title: Event logs and Kafka
summary: A log keeps every event in order after it is read, so many consumers can read it at their own pace and replay it from the start.

blocks.p: A queue deletes a message once it is processed. That is fine for jobs. But some data is useful long after it first arrives.
A new analytics service wants every order from the last week. A bug in the search indexer means its index must be rebuilt from scratch. With a queue, those events are gone.

An **event log** is an append-only list of events. Producers add events to the end. Nothing is changed in place, and reading an event doesn't remove it. The log keeps events for a set time, such as a week, or forever.
Each event has an **offset**, its position in the log. A consumer keeps track of the offset it has reached. To read again from the start, it moves its offset back.

One log on one machine has a limit. So a **topic** is split into **partitions**, separate logs that can live on different machines. Each event goes to a partition chosen by a hash of its key, such as the user ID.
Order is kept within a partition, not across the topic. Events with the same key always land in the same partition, so all of one user's events stay in order.

A **consumer group** is one reader of the topic, such as billing. It keeps its own offset in each partition. Two groups read the same events without affecting each other. Inside a group, each partition is read by one consumer, so the number of partitions limits how many consumers a group can use.

blocks.caption: Events from four users go into three partitions by key. Each group has its own offset in each partition, shown by the triangles. A group that starts late reads everything from offset 0.

blocks.p: Keeping events costs disk. The log stores each event once per copy, for as long as retention says.

blocks.caption: Disk needed for a topic, from event rate, event size, retention and copies.

list: **Kafka is the common event log.** Its [documentation](https://kafka.apache.org/intro#main-concepts-and-terminology) describes topics split into partitions, events with the same key going to the same partition, and order kept per partition.
**Retention is a setting.** Kafka keeps events for a configured time or size. The broker default for `log.retention.hours` is 168, which is 7 days.

**Compaction keeps the latest value per key.** With [log compaction](https://kafka.apache.org/44/design/design/#log-compaction), Kafka keeps at least the last event for each key, so a topic can hold the current state of every record.

**The log as the source of truth.** Jay Kreps' [The Log](https://engineering.linkedin.com/distributed-systems/log-what-every-software-engineer-should-know-about-real-time-datas-unifying) explains how a shared log lets many systems build their own views of the same data.
**Choose the key with care.** One very busy key puts all its events in one partition, and that partition becomes the bottleneck, as in the sharding lesson.
An event log appends events and keeps them after they are read.
Each consumer group tracks its own offset, so groups read independently and can replay from the start.
Topics are split into partitions by key. Order holds within a partition, and the partition count limits a group's consumers.
Retention sets how long events are kept, and so how much disk the topic needs.
